name: Chapter 2: Human Reproduction
description: Male and female reproductive systems, gametogenesis, menstrual cycle, fertilisation, implantation, pregnancy, parturition and lactation

cards.definition: Sexually reproducing and viviparous

cards.text: Reproductive events in order: {{c1::gametogenesis}} → {{c2::insemination}} → {{c3::fertilisation}} → blastocyst formation and {{c4::implantation}} → {{c5::gestation}} → {{c6::parturition}}.

cards.term: Male vs female difference in gamete formation with age?
cards.definition: Sperm formation continues even in old men; ovum formation ceases around 50 years

cards.term: Where is the male reproductive system located?
cards.definition: In the pelvis region

cards.term: Components of the male reproductive system?
cards.definition: A pair of testes, accessory ducts, accessory glands and external genitalia
Outside the abdominal cavity in a pouch called the scrotum
Keeps testes 2–2.5 °C lower than body temperature, needed for spermatogenesis
Oval; 4–5 cm long, 2–3 cm wide

cards.term: How many testicular lobules per testis?
cards.definition: About 250

cards.term: What does each testicular lobule contain?
cards.definition: One to three highly coiled seminiferous tubules, where sperms are produced

cards.term: Two cell types lining a seminiferous tubule?
cards.definition: Male germ cells (spermatogonia) and Sertoli cells
Provide nutrition to the germ cells
Small blood vessels, interstitial (Leydig) cells and other immunologically competent cells
Synthesise and secrete androgens (testicular hormones)
Interstitial cells, spermatogonia, spermatozoa, Sertoli cells (T.S. of seminiferous tubules)

cards.text: Male accessory ducts (in order of sperm flow): seminiferous tubules → {{c1::rete testis}} → {{c2::vasa efferentia}} → {{c3::epididymis}} → {{c4::vas deferens}} → ejaculatory duct → urethra.

cards.definition: Along the posterior surface of each testis

Ascends to the abdomen
Loops over the urinary bladder
Receives the seminal vesicle duct
Opens into the urethra as the ejaculatory duct

cards.term: Function of the male accessory ducts?
cards.definition: Store and transport sperms from testis to the outside through the urethra
The external opening of the urethra at the tip of the penis

cards.term: What is the glans penis and what covers it?
cards.definition: Enlarged end of the penis, covered by a loose fold of skin, the foreskin
Paired seminal vesicles, a prostate, paired bulbourethral glands
Fructose, calcium and certain enzymes

cards.term: Extra function of bulbourethral gland secretion?
cards.definition: Lubrication of the penis
It is the fuel for sperm mitochondria that power the tail

cards.term: Parts of the female reproductive system?
cards.definition: Pair of ovaries, pair of oviducts, uterus, cervix, vagina, external genitalia (plus mammary glands)

cards.term: Processes supported by the female reproductive system?
cards.definition: Ovulation, fertilisation, pregnancy, birth and child care

cards.term: Primary female sex organs, and their products?
cards.definition: Ovaries: the ovum and several steroid hormones (ovarian hormones)

cards.term: Size of an ovary, and how is it held in place?
cards.definition: 2–4 cm long; connected to the pelvic wall and uterus by ligaments
Covered by thin epithelium enclosing the ovarian stroma, divided into outer cortex and inner medulla
Oviducts (fallopian tubes), uterus, vagina
10–12 cm

cards.text: Parts of the fallopian tube from ovary to uterus: {{c1::infundibulum}} (funnel with fimbriae) → {{c2::ampulla}} (wider) → {{c3::isthmus}} (narrow lumen, joins uterus).

cards.definition: Finger-like projections of the infundibulum that collect the ovum after ovulation

cards.term: Other name and shape of the uterus?
cards.definition: Womb; shaped like an inverted pear
Cervical canal + vagina

cards.text: Uterine wall, outside to inside: {{c1::perimetrium}} (thin membrane) → {{c2::myometrium}} (thick smooth muscle) → {{c3::endometrium}} (glandular).

cards.term: Which uterine layer changes cyclically, and which contracts in delivery?
cards.definition: Endometrium: cyclical changes in menstrual cycle. Myometrium: strong contractions in delivery.
Mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, hymen, clitoris
Cushion of fatty tissue covered by skin and pubic hair

Majora: fleshy folds from the mons pubis surrounding the vaginal opening
Minora: paired folds under the labia majora
Membrane often partially covering the vaginal opening

cards.term: What is the clitoris, and where is it?
cards.definition: Tiny finger-like structure at the upper junction of the two labia minora, above the urethral opening

cards.term: Is the hymen a reliable indicator of virginity?
cards.definition: No. It can tear from a fall, tampon, sports (cycling, horse riding) or may persist after coitus
Female pelvis (side view): uterus, urinary bladder, pubic symphysis, urethra, clitoris, labia, vaginal orifice, cervix, rectum, vagina, anus
All female mammals (functional mammary gland)

cards.term: Number of mammary lobes per breast?
cards.definition: 15–20 lobes containing clusters of cells called alveoli

cards.text: Milk path: {{c1::alveoli}} → {{c2::mammary tubules}} → {{c3::mammary duct}} → {{c4::mammary ampulla}} → {{c5::lactiferous duct}} → nipple.

cards.definition: Production of gametes (sperms, ovum) by the primary sex organs
At puberty

cards.term: How do spermatogonia increase in number?
cards.definition: By mitotic division on the inside wall of seminiferous tubules
Diploid, 46
Spermatogonia that periodically undergo meiosis (2n = 46)

cards.term: Result of meiosis I in a primary spermatocyte?
cards.definition: Two equal haploid secondary spermatocytes (23 chromosomes each)

cards.term: Result of meiosis II in secondary spermatocytes?
cards.definition: Four equal haploid spermatids (23 chromosomes)
Transformation of spermatids into spermatozoa
Release of sperms from the seminiferous tubules (after heads are embedded in Sertoli cells)
Spermio-GENESIS = making the sperm shape. Spermi-ATION = sperm leaves (like "evacuation").

cards.term: Why does spermatogenesis start at puberty?
cards.definition: Significant increase in GnRH secretion by the hypothalamus
Acts on Leydig cells → androgen secretion → stimulates spermatogenesis
Acts on Sertoli cells → secretes factors that help spermiogenesis
GnRH, LH, FSH, androgens

Androgens are produced by Sertoli cells: False: by Leydig cells; Spermatozoa get nutrition from Sertoli cells: True; Leydig cells are found in the ovary: False: in the testis; Oogenesis takes place in corpus luteum: False: in the ovary (follicles); Menstrual cycle ceases during pregnancy: True

cards.text: A sperm has a {{c1::head}}, {{c2::neck}}, {{c3::middle piece}} and {{c4::tail}}, all enveloped by a plasma membrane.

cards.term: What does the sperm head contain?
cards.definition: An elongated haploid nucleus, capped anteriorly by the acrosome
Filled with enzymes that help fertilisation of the ovum
Numerous mitochondria produce energy for tail movement (sperm motility)
200–300 million
At least 60% sperms of normal shape and size, and at least 40% with vigorous motility

cards.term: Secretions essential for sperm maturation and motility?
cards.definition: Of the epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle and prostate
Seminal plasma + sperms

cards.term: What maintains the male accessory ducts and glands?
cards.definition: Androgens (testicular hormones)
Formation of a mature female gamete
During embryonic development: a couple of million oogonia form in each fetal ovary
No
An oogonium that enters prophase-I of meiosis and is arrested there
A primary oocyte surrounded by a layer of granulosa cells

cards.term: Primary follicles left in each ovary at puberty?
cards.definition: 60,000–80,000 (many degenerate from birth to puberty)
Primary follicle with more layers of granulosa cells and a new theca
A fluid-filled cavity, the antrum; theca splits into theca interna and theca externa

cards.term: When does the primary oocyte complete meiosis I?
cards.definition: Inside the tertiary follicle

cards.term: Products of meiosis I in oogenesis?
cards.definition: Unequal: a large haploid secondary oocyte and a tiny first polar body

cards.term: Advantage of unequal division in oogenesis? (think)
cards.definition: The secondary oocyte keeps the bulk of nutrient-rich cytoplasm for the early embryo

cards.term: New membrane formed around the secondary oocyte?
cards.definition: Zona pellucida
Rupture of the Graafian follicle releasing the secondary oocyte (ovum)

cards.term: At what stage is the "ovum" released in humans?
cards.definition: As a secondary oocyte (arrested in meiosis II); meiosis II completes only after sperm entry
"P-S-T-G": Primary → Secondary → Tertiary → Graafian → (after ovulation) corpus luteum

cards.term: Read the schematic: chromosome number at each stage (Figure 2.8)?
cards.definition: Spermatogonia/oogonia and primary cells: 46; secondary cells, spermatids/ovum: 23
Begins: Puberty vs embryonic life; Divisions: Equal vs unequal (polar bodies); Products per mother cell: 4 sperms vs 1 ovum + polar bodies; Duration: Continues into old age vs stops at menopause

cards.term: Does the first polar body divide further?
cards.definition: NCERT: not certain. Update: in humans it often degenerates without dividing, though in some cases it divides.

cards.term: What is the menstrual cycle, and in which animals?
cards.definition: Reproductive cycle of female primates (monkeys, apes, humans)
The first menstruation, at puberty

cards.term: Average length of the human menstrual cycle?
cards.definition: 28/29 days

cards.term: How many ova are released per cycle, and when?
cards.definition: One, in the middle of the cycle

cards.term: Duration and cause of the menstrual phase?
cards.definition: 3–5 days; breakdown of the endometrial lining and its blood vessels
Only if the released ovum is not fertilised
Pregnancy; also stress, poor health etc.
Primary follicles grow into a Graafian follicle; endometrium regenerates by proliferation
LH and FSH rise gradually; growing follicles secrete estrogens

cards.term: When do LH and FSH peak?
cards.definition: Mid-cycle, about 14th day

cards.term: What is the LH surge and what does it do?
cards.definition: Rapid mid-cycle LH rise that induces rupture of the Graafian follicle → ovulation

cards.term: What happens in the luteal (secretory) phase?
cards.definition: Remains of the Graafian follicle become the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone

cards.term: Function of progesterone from the corpus luteum?
cards.definition: Maintains the endometrium, needed for implantation and pregnancy

cards.term: What happens to the corpus luteum without fertilisation?
cards.definition: It degenerates → endometrium disintegrates → menstruation
Cessation of menstrual cycles around 50 years
Normal reproductive phase, between menarche and menopause

cards.term: Read the chart (Figure 2.9): which hormone peaks in the luteal phase?
cards.definition: Progesterone (estrogen has a smaller second rise)

Menstrual phase: Days 1–5: endometrium sheds; Follicular phase: Days 5–13: follicle grows, estrogen rises; Ovulatory phase: Day 14: LH surge, ovulation; Luteal phase: Days 15–28: corpus luteum, progesterone

Days and key event?

Menstrual phase?
Follicular phase?
Ovulatory phase?
Luteal phase?
advancedHtml.backHtml:

Days and key event?

Menstrual phaseDays 1–5: endometrium sheds
Follicular phaseDays 5–13: follicle grows, estrogen rises
Ovulatory phaseDay 14: LH surge, ovulation
Luteal phaseDays 15–28: corpus luteum, progesterone

cards.definition: "My Friend Offers Lunch": Menstrual, Follicular, Ovulatory, Luteal

cards.term: Menstrual hygiene: how often to change pads?
cards.definition: Every 4–5 hours as required dispose wrapped in paper, never in drains wash hands with soap
Release of semen by the penis into the vagina during coitus
In the ampullary region of the fallopian tube

cards.term: Why doesn’t every copulation lead to pregnancy?
cards.definition: Ovum and sperm must reach the ampulla simultaneously

cards.term: How does the ovum ensure only one sperm enters?
cards.definition: The sperm contacting the zona pellucida induces membrane changes that block additional sperms

cards.term: Identify the layers around the ovum (Figure 2.10).
cards.definition: Zona pellucida, corona radiata cells, perivitelline space

cards.term: Role of acrosome secretions in fertilisation?
cards.definition: Help the sperm enter the ovum cytoplasm through the zona pellucida and plasma membrane

cards.term: What does sperm entry trigger in the secondary oocyte?
cards.definition: Completion of meiosis II → second polar body + haploid ovum (ootid)
46 (diploid)

cards.term: Why is the baby’s sex decided by the father?
cards.definition: All ova carry X; 50% sperms carry X and 50% carry Y. XX → girl, XY → boy.

cards.term: What is cleavage and where does it start?
cards.definition: Mitotic divisions of the zygote as it moves through the isthmus towards the uterus
The daughter cells (2, 4, 8, 16…) formed by cleavage
Embryo with 8–16 blastomeres
Outer trophoblast and inner cell mass

cards.term: Fate of trophoblast and inner cell mass?
cards.definition: Trophoblast: attaches to endometrium. Inner cell mass: differentiates into the embryo.
Blastocyst becomes embedded in the endometrium (uterine cells cover it); leads to pregnancy

cards.term: Trace the journey: fertilisation to implantation (Figure 2.11).
cards.definition: Ovum → fertilised in ampulla → zygote → cleavage → morula → blastocyst → implantation in uterus

cards.term: Correction: NCERT says "the embryo with 8 to 16 blastomeres is called a morula". Is 8–16 cells precise?
cards.definition: Exam answer: 8–16. Update: a morula usually has about 16–32 cells; the 8–16 figure is a simplification.
Finger-like projections of the trophoblast after implantation, surrounded by uterine tissue and maternal blood
Structural and functional unit between embryo and mother formed by chorionic villi + uterine tissue
Supplies O₂ and nutrients, removes CO₂ and wastes, and acts as an endocrine tissue

cards.term: What connects the placenta to the embryo?
cards.definition: The umbilical cord
hCG, hPL, estrogens, progestogens

cards.term: Hormone secreted by the ovary late in pregnancy?
cards.definition: Relaxin
hCG, hPL and relaxin

cards.term: Hormones increased several-fold in maternal blood during pregnancy?
cards.definition: Estrogens, progestogens, cortisol, prolactin, thyroxine

cards.term: Why do pregnancy tests detect hCG? (intuition)
cards.definition: hCG is made only in pregnancy (by the placenta), so its presence in urine signals pregnancy

cards.text: After implantation the inner cell mass forms outer {{c1::ectoderm}} and inner {{c2::endoderm}}; {{c3::mesoderm}} appears between them.

cards.term: What are stem cells of the inner cell mass?
cards.definition: Cells with potency to give rise to all tissues and organs

End of month 1: Heart forms; End of month 2: Limbs and digits; End of 12 weeks (1st trimester): Most major organ systems; limbs and external genitals well developed; Month 5: First movements, hair on head; End of 24 weeks (2nd trimester): Fine body hair, eyelids separate, eyelashes

cards.term: First sign of a growing foetus by stethoscope?
cards.definition: The heart sound (heart forms after one month)
Placental villi, umbilical cord with vessels, cavity of uterus, yolk sac, embryo, plug of mucus in cervix
About 9 months
Delivery of the foetus (childbirth) by vigorous uterine contraction
A complex neuroendocrine mechanism

cards.term: What is the foetal ejection reflex?
cards.definition: Mild uterine contractions triggered by signals from the fully developed foetus and placenta

1) Foetal ejection reflex
2) Oxytocin from maternal pituitary
3) Stronger contractions → more oxytocin
4) Expulsion of baby, then placenta

cards.term: Why is parturition an example of positive feedback? (intuition)
cards.definition: Contraction increases oxytocin, which increases contraction: the loop amplifies until birth

cards.term: What do doctors inject to induce delivery?
cards.definition: Oxytocin
Cortisol, estrogens and oxytocin
Milk production by mammary glands towards the end of pregnancy/after birth

cards.term: What is colostrum and why is it important?
cards.definition: Milk of the first few days; contains antibodies (IgA) that give the newborn resistance

Release of ovum from mature follicle: Ovulation; Ovulation is induced by: LH; Fertilisation takes place in: Ampulla of fallopian tube; Zygote divides to form (implanted): Blastocyst; Vascular connection between foetus and uterus: Placenta

cards.term: Mother gave birth to identical twins: how many eggs released? Fraternal twins? (Exercise 20)
cards.definition: Identical: one egg (the embryo splits). Fraternal: two eggs.

cards.term: A female dog gave birth to 6 puppies. Minimum eggs released? (Exercise 21)
cards.definition: Six (dogs are multiovulatory)

cards.term: Two functions each of testis and ovary? (Exercise 4)
cards.definition: Testis: sperms, androgens. Ovary: ovum, estrogen and progesterone.
